introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0, Al = 27.0, S = 32.0, Na = 23.0, Fe = 56.

The paper is arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry; Section B - Inorganic Chemistry; Section C - Organic Chemistry.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A 5.00 g sample of the ore was reacted with excess concentrated hydrochloric acid and filtered. The filtrate was made up to $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ in a volumetric flask with distilled water. A $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ sample of the standard solution required $27.30\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.020\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ dichromate (VI) solution for complete reaction.

Calculate:

(i) the amount, in moles, of dichromate (VI) ions used in the titration.

(ii) the amount, in moles, of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ions present in $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of solution

(iii) the mass of iron (II) carbonate present in the ore.

(iv) the percentage of iron (II) carbonate in the sample *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Amount of dichromate (VI).** $n = c \times V = 0.020\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \times \dfrac{27.30}{1000}\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 5.46 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

**(ii) Amount of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ in $25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.** From the equation, $1\ \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ reacts with $6\ \mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$:

$n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}) = 6 \times 5.46 \times 10^{-4} = 3.276 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ (that is $3.28 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$).

**(iii) Mass of $\mathrm{FeCO_3}$ in the ore.** The $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ sample is one tenth of the $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ solution, so the whole solution contains

$n(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}) = 10 \times 3.276 \times 10^{-3} = 3.276 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

All the iron(II) came from $\mathrm{FeCO_3}$ (1 mol $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ per mol $\mathrm{FeCO_3}$), so $n(\mathrm{FeCO_3}) = 3.276 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

$M(\mathrm{FeCO_3}) = 56 + 12.0 + 3 \times 16.0 = 116\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

$m = 3.276 \times 10^{-2} \times 116 = 3.80\ \mathrm{g}$

**(iv) Percentage of $\mathrm{FeCO_3}$ in the sample.**

$\% = \dfrac{3.80}{5.00} \times 100 = 76.0\ \%$

(The ore sample therefore contains $76.0\ \%$ of iron (II) carbonate by mass.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
What do you understand by

(i) Relative atomic mass?

(ii) Isotopes? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Relative atomic mass** ($A_r$) is the **weighted mean (average) mass of an atom of the element, taking account of the relative abundance of its isotopes, relative to $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of an atom of carbon-12**. It has no unit.

**(ii) Isotopes** are **atoms of the same element (same number of protons, same atomic number) that have different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers**. They have the same chemical properties (same electronic configuration) but slightly different physical properties, for example mass. Example: $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Consider the diagram of a mass spectrometer below.

![fig-1](gce-al-chemistry-2020-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

(i) On the diagram, label the parts A to D

(ii) State what happens at A, B and C *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Labels** (reading of the diagram: A marks the first chamber where the sample enters, B the pair of plates and slits just after it, C the shaded curved region, D the evacuated tube after the curved region that ends at the box marked DETECTION):

| Label | Part of the mass spectrometer |
|---|---|
| A | **Ionisation chamber** (ion source), where the vaporised sample is introduced |
| B | **Accelerating electric field**: charged, perforated plates (slits) |
| C | **Magnetic field** (electromagnet): the deflection region |
| D | **Path of the deflected ions** (evacuated flight tube) leading to the **detector** (ion collector) |

**(ii) What happens at A, B and C.**

- **A (ionisation):** the sample is vaporised at low pressure and bombarded with a beam of high-energy electrons, which knock an electron out of each atom or molecule to give positive ions: $\mathrm{X(g)} + \mathrm{e^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{X^+(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^-}$.
- **B (acceleration):** the positive ions are attracted towards the negatively charged plates, **accelerated by an electric field** to a high speed and collimated by the slits into a narrow beam.
- **C (deflection):** the beam passes through a **magnetic field** which deflects the ions along a circular path. The radius depends on the mass/charge ratio ($m/z$): lighter ions (or ions with a higher charge) are deflected more. For a given field strength only ions of one $m/z$ follow the path that reaches the detector; by varying the field each isotope is brought to the detector in turn.

At the detector (end of path D) the ion current is recorded, which gives the relative abundance of each isotope (and so the relative atomic mass).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The following results were obtained when determining the rate of the reaction

$2\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{NOCl(g)}$

| Expt | $[\mathrm{NO}]\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ | $[\mathrm{Cl_2}]\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ | Initial rate $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.17 |
| 2 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.35 |
| 3 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 1.45 |

(i) Determine the overall order of the reaction above showing all the steps

(ii) Consider the reaction below $2\mathrm{N_2O_5(g)} \rightarrow 4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$. The mechanism for the reaction is given as:

$2\mathrm{N_2O_5(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{N_2O_3(g)} + 2\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \tfrac{5}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)}$ - Slow step

$\mathrm{N_2O_3(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ - Fast step

$\mathrm{NO(g)} + 2\mathrm{N_2O_5(g)} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{N_2O_5(g)}$ - Fast step

Write down the rate equation for the reaction *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Overall order.** Write $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^{x}[\mathrm{Cl_2}]^{y}$.

*Order with respect to $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ (compare experiments 1 and 2).* $[\mathrm{NO}]$ is constant at $0.10$ and $[\mathrm{Cl_2}]$ doubles ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.20$). The rate rises from $0.17$ to $0.35$, a factor of $\dfrac{0.35}{0.17} = 2.06 \approx 2$. So $2^{y} = 2$ and $y = 1$: the reaction is **first order in $\mathrm{Cl_2}$**.

*Order with respect to NO (compare experiments 2 and 3).* $[\mathrm{Cl_2}]$ is constant at $0.20$ and $[\mathrm{NO}]$ doubles ($0.10 \rightarrow 0.20$). The rate rises from $0.35$ to $1.45$, a factor of $\dfrac{1.45}{0.35} = 4.14 \approx 4$. So $2^{x} = 4$ and $x = 2$: the reaction is **second order in NO**.

Rate equation: $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{NO}]^{2}[\mathrm{Cl_2}]$.

**Overall order $= 2 + 1 = 3$** (third order).

(Check with experiment 1: $k = \dfrac{0.17}{(0.10)^2(0.10)} = 1.7 \times 10^{2}\ \mathrm{mol^{-2}\,dm^{6}\,s^{-1}}$; experiment 3 gives $\dfrac{1.45}{(0.20)^2(0.20)} = 1.8 \times 10^{2}$, the same within experimental error.)

**(ii) Rate equation.** The rate of a reaction is controlled by its **slow (rate-determining) step**. In the mechanism as printed the slow step involves **two molecules of $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$** and nothing else, and the two fast steps that follow do not appear in the rate equation. The orders are therefore the coefficients of the reactants in the slow step:

$$\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]^{2}$$

(The reaction is second order overall, following the printed mechanism. See the remark on the printed steps in the uncertainties: experimentally, the decomposition of $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$ is first order.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the reaction below and answer the questions that follow.

$\mathrm{N_2O_4} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}$  $\Delta H = +243\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

How does an increase in temperature affect:

A: Equilibrium position

B: Equilibrium constant of the above reaction *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The forward reaction is **endothermic** ($\Delta H$ positive).

**A. Equilibrium position:** by Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature makes the system oppose the change by absorbing heat, so the **equilibrium position shifts to the right** (the endothermic direction): more $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and less $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ at equilibrium.

**B. Equilibrium constant:** $K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2O_4}]}$ **increases** with temperature, because the concentration of the product rises relative to that of the reactant. (For an endothermic reaction $K$ always increases when $T$ increases.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the acid/base conjugate pairs in the reaction below.

$\mathrm{C_6H_5COO^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH(aq)} + \mathrm{OH^-(aq)}$ *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Bronsted-Lowry theory an acid donates a proton and its conjugate base is what remains; the two members of a pair differ by one proton.

- $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (acid) and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ (its conjugate base);
- $\mathrm{C_6H_5COO^-}$ (base, which accepts a proton from water) and $\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$ (its conjugate acid).

Conjugate pairs: **$\mathrm{H_2O}$ / $\mathrm{OH^-}$** and **$\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}$ / $\mathrm{C_6H_5COO^-}$**.
